QMSBR—*Quantitative Methods for Social and Behavioral Research*—is a modular
collection of chapters designed to support more than one quantitative-methods
course. Its primary purpose is to help applied researchers read quantitative
studies; evaluating a study and learning how to conduct a clearer one are
secondary benefits. The collection is maintained as one canonical library so a
correction can improve every course route that uses it.

<span id="the-framework"></span>

## The argument-based approach {#the-approach}

A finalized quantitative study can be read as a **question--answer contract**.
The research question declares what answer is owed. Methods, results,
supplemental materials, and reservations provide the record from which a reader
decides whether the final answer is warranted.

The basic rule is deliberately simple: **one question--answer pair has one
argument**. That argument has linked statistical and substantive layers. A
study with several separable questions needs several arguments; shared data do
not erase question-specific obligations.

| Component | Statistical layer | Substantive layer |
|---|---|---|
| **Evidence (E)** | Recorded observations and how they were produced | What those records represent in their setting, population, and period |
| **Justification (J)** | Why the design, measurement, and procedure can address the statistical target | Why the contextualized evidence bears on the substantive question |
| **Inference (I)** | Estimate or prediction, uncertainty, checking, sensitivity, and analytic status | Meaning, magnitude, importance, alternatives, and scope |
| **Bounded Claim (C)** | A qualified statistical result | The final bounded answer, including reservations |

Within each layer, Evidence and Justification jointly support Inference, which
supports a bounded Claim: **E + J → I → C**. Across layers, the substantive
components situate, evaluate, interpret, and bound their statistical
counterparts. The statistical layer is therefore not a second argument, and a
software result is not the whole inference.

The basic chapter also introduces two supporting extensions. A six-stage,
two-phase **construction workflow** describes how one simple argument may be
built. Iteration stays within its current phase; changing a Phase 1 commitment
after Phase 2 has begun starts a new or revised cycle, although valid work may be
reused. Six **evaluation questions** test question alignment, evidence integrity,
justification adequacy, inferential adequacy, transition fidelity, and claim
calibration. Authors evaluate first, but collaborators, reviewers, editors, and
readers also have independent responsibility; the questions produce a reasoned
profile, not a mechanical score.

Chapter 1 is the sole common prerequisite for the series. The optional Chapter
1a extends the approach to coordinated questions, an eight-stage workflow,
cross-question coherence, and regression-based methods. Regression can
instantiate targets, estimates, contrasts, and checks, but it cannot by itself
supply construct meaning, representative evidence, or a causal design.

The approach is **Toulmin-informed**: it retains evidence, justified inferential
bridges, qualified claims, and explicit reservations without treating the eight
components as one-to-one replacements for Toulmin's roles. LeMire (2010)
provides a related statistical precedent focused on null-hypothesis testing.

## Scope

Part One focuses mainly on observable variables and foundational statistical
reasoning. Chapters 1--4 keep the learner route code-independent; later chapters
introduce reproducible computing and regression when those tools serve a clear
reading or research purpose. Factor analysis and latent-variable modelling are
reserved for Part Two; multilevel and longitudinal models are reserved for Part
Three. Study design is addressed wherever it controls interpretation, but a
named statistical procedure never creates a causal claim.

## Using QMSBR in a course {#courses}

QMSBR is a source library, not a syllabus. Keep chapter identities stable and
let each course choose its own sequence and assessed work.

| QMSBR website | Your course space |
|---|---|
| Canonical current chapters | The term sequence and weekly instructions |
| Stable public links | Announcements and deadlines |
| Answer-free chapter exercises | Assessment, feedback, and answer keys |

Link to the website so students receive corrections automatically. Lecture
notes, solutions, and assessments stay in your own course space.

## Accessibility

HTML is the preferred reading format: it provides responsive layout, headings,
search, link text, and selectable code. Downloadable PDFs are retained for
printing and annotation and are checked for reading order, document language,
bookmarks, metadata, and visual integrity. Accessibility problems can be
reported through the repository issue tracker or by email.
